title: Eisenkot given tough task of forming Israeli government over Netanyahu
gist: Gadi Eisenkot received Herzog's mandate (initial 28-day deadline) to form a government replacing Netanyahu, backed by 67 recommendations that rely on a record Israeli-Arab seat haul; Liberman's refusal to ally with Arab parties and his pivot toward the ultra-Orthodox make the path fragile, with a 48-seat minority government a possible but weak start.

insights.claim: Former military chief Gadi Eisenkot was set to receive President Isaac Herzog's mandate to form an Israeli government with an initial deadline of 28 days, aiming to replace Benjamin Netanyahu.
insights.speaker: Al-Monitor
insights.so_what: The 28-day clock sets the window for Israeli political-risk resolution.

insights.claim: In consultations with Herzog, Eisenkot received recommendations from parties accounting for 67 lawmakers versus 46 for Netanyahu, after Netanyahu lost support in the October 2026 election with no side winning an outright majority.
insights.speaker: Al-Monitor
insights.so_what: Netanyahu's era may be ending, but the opposition majority is fragile.
insights.locator: In consultations last week with Herzog

insights.claim: Eisenkot's 67-seat count includes Israeli Arab parties, whose seat haul surged to a historic high on anger over Netanyahu's government with far-right figures who sought to marginalise the community.
insights.speaker: Al-Monitor
insights.so_what: Arab-party dependence is the key fault line determining whether an Eisenkot coalition is viable.
insights.quote: whose seat haul surged to a historic high on anger over Netanyahu's government
insights.locator: But the vote count included Israeli Arabs

insights.claim: Avigdor Liberman, whose party has seven seats, remains adamant he will never ally with Israeli Arabs, blocking the simplest route to an Eisenkot majority.
insights.speaker: Al-Monitor
insights.so_what: Liberman is the swing veto; his stance raises deadlock and repeat-election odds.
insights.quote: I will not lend a hand to the establishment of such a government, which in my view will harm security and bring Netanyahu back to power

insights.claim: Liberman reversed a signature campaign pledge by signaling openness to an alliance with ultra-Orthodox parties, whose two main parties had backed Netanyahu but could push Eisenkot to a majority.
insights.speaker: Al-Monitor
insights.so_what: An Eisenkot–Haredi deal would likely preserve military-service exemptions, a fiscal and social flashpoint.
insights.locator: Taking back one of his signature

insights.claim: The ultra-Orthodox military-service exemption is a growing source of resentment among Israelis as reservists serve multiple tours of duty in multi-front wars.
insights.speaker: Al-Monitor
insights.so_what: Reservist burden is a labor-supply and fiscal drag on Israel's economy; exemption politics drive coalition stability.

insights.claim: Liberman said he must make 'difficult decisions' to prioritize ousting Netanyahu, who faces corruption charges that could land him in jail if he loses power.
insights.speaker: Al-Monitor
insights.so_what: Netanyahu's personal legal exposure gives him strong incentive to fight to retain power, prolonging instability.
insights.locator: Liberman said Sunday he still backed

insights.claim: Liberman denied speculation that he was trying to engineer a deadlock that could make him prime minister.
insights.speaker: Al-Monitor
insights.so_what: Market observers suspect kingmaker gamesmanship; watch for deadlock scenarios.
insights.locator: Liberman, whose party at seven votes

insights.claim: Naftali Bennett, also outspoken against the ultra-Orthodox military exemption, has stayed quiet since Liberman's about-face.
insights.speaker: Al-Monitor
insights.so_what: Bennett's position on a Haredi alliance is a second coalition swing factor.

insights.claim: Eisenkot rules out a unity government with Netanyahu and calls for a 'national emergency' government, describing Netanyahu as a fundamental threat to Israeli democracy.
insights.speaker: Al-Monitor
insights.so_what: No unity option narrows coalition paths and increases the chance of a minority government or new elections.
insights.quote: a fundamental threat to the very existence of Israeli democracy

insights.claim: Eisenkot appears willing to start with a minority government relying on outside votes from Israeli-Arab parties while seeking a stable majority.
insights.speaker: Al-Monitor
insights.so_what: A minority government would be legislatively weak—budget and reform passage would be slow.

insights.claim: Israel Democracy Institute expert Assaf Shapira says an Eisenkot government with only 48 lawmakers would be especially fragile and forced into extensive negotiations on every piece of legislation.
insights.speaker: Al-Monitor
insights.so_what: Expect policy paralysis risk under a minority government, relevant for Israeli fiscal policy and bonds.
insights.quote: To pass laws, you need strong support from other parties

insights.claim: Eisenkot has warned Netanyahu he lacks a mandate for another attack on Iran, though he has largely backed Netanyahu's war decisions.
insights.speaker: Al-Monitor
insights.so_what: A government change could lower odds of renewed Israeli strikes on Iran, but not a dovish pivot overall.
insights.quote: he does not have the mandate for another attack on Iran

insights.claim: Eisenkot has vowed to repair Israel's international reputation and end extremist settler violence against Palestinians in the West Bank.
insights.speaker: Al-Monitor
insights.so_what: Improved reputation could ease sanctions/boycott pressure and support Israel risk assets.

insights.claim: As military commander in the 2006 war with Hezbollah, Eisenkot devised the 'Dahiya doctrine' of massive force against civilian infrastructure where enemies operate, which critics call a war crime.
insights.speaker: Al-Monitor
insights.so_what: Eisenkot is no dove on security; don't assume softer posture toward Hezbollah.

insights.claim: Eisenkot, born to working-class Moroccan immigrants, would be Israel's first Sephardic prime minister in a country long dominated by an Ashkenazi elite.
insights.speaker: Al-Monitor
insights.so_what: Symbolic shift in Israel's political elite.

insights.claim: A Tel Aviv voter said that even if Eisenkot forms a government, it won't solve Israel's deeper internal conflict.
insights.speaker: Al-Monitor
insights.so_what: Polarisation persists beyond any coalition outcome.
insights.quote: even if he manages to form a government, it won't solve the underlying issues
